meta.task: M1-19 / M5 — sourced dog data for realism
meta.status: Imported into breed_stage_params (M5-R01, BreedStageParamsSeeder). Game values David confirmed on 2026-10-05 carry a "decision" field. M5-R03 (2026-10-06): training values added (learning multiplier, individual variation — David decisions; minutes, progress, decay, effects — proposals). M5-R03b (2026-10-06): David confirmed minutes, progress and decay; starting progress per arrival stage added (decision); the two effects stay proposals.

conventions.confidence: high = breed standard / peer-reviewed / vet association and consistent across sources; medium = single reputable source or sources disagree a little; low = secondary source, strong disagreement, or derived/proposal
conventions.unsourced: Anything with source_id null is marked 'UNSOURCED — proposal' and must not be shown to parents/children as fact.
conventions.quotes: Quotes are as returned by the web-fetch tool on 2026-10-05; spot-check against the URL before import.
conventions.game_time: 1 real week = 1 month of dog age (REALISM_SPEC §2).
conventions.decision: "potrdil David 2026-10-05: …" = the game value David confirmed (DECISIONS 2026-10-05). It is a product decision, NOT literature: source_id stays the underlying evidence and is null where the literature gives no number.

salt_2017_bands_kg.quote: Category I: <6.5 kg … Category IV: 15 to <30 kg; Category V: 30 to <40 kg
salt_2017_bands_kg.notes: Category IV breeds: Australian Shepherd, Chow Chow, Basset Hound, Siberian Husky, English Bulldog, Pit Bull type, Boxer. Border Collie not listed.

puppy.quote: From birth to cessation of rapid growth (~6–9 months, varying with breed and size)

young_adult.quote: From cessation of rapid growth to completion of physical and social maturation, which occurs in most dogs by 3 to 4 years of age
young_adult.notes: AAHA has no separate 'adolescent' stage; it is inside 'young adult'.
young_adult.decision: potrdil David 2026-10-05: young stage starts at 9 months (upper end of ~6–9 months)

adolescence.quote: dog adolescence (which typically begins between six to nine months of age) … during puberty (at around eight months of age)
adolescence.notes: Press summary of Asher & Harvey, Biology Letters 2020 (guide-dog puppies, n=285). End of adolescence not stated.

mature_adult.value: 3–4 years → start of last 25% of lifespan
mature_adult.quote: From completion of physical and social maturation until the last 25% of estimated lifespan (breed and size dependent)
mature_adult.decision: potrdil David 2026-10-05: adult stage starts at 36 months (lower end of 3–4 years)

senior.quote: From the last 25% of estimated lifespan through end-of-life.

senior_rule_of_thumb.quote: Dogs over the age of seven can be considered 'senior' … dogs aged over 12 can be considered 'geriatric.'
senior_rule_of_thumb.notes: UK charity rule of thumb, not size-specific; conflicts with AAHA 25% rule for long-lived dogs.

adult_weight_reached_by_size.quote: very small dogs reaching maturity at between 8 and 12 months of age and larger breeds requiring up to 24 months to reach adult body weight

growth_end_by_size_class.notes: Growth stops when growth plates seal (S10); no plate-closure ages given.

growth_plate_closure.notes: UNSOURCED — proposal. No veterinary source with plate-closure ages per size was found; use 'growth_end_by_size_class' instead.

logistic_model.description: Logistic curve y = a / (1 + exp(-(x - x0)/b)), x in weeks. Shape parameters = arithmetic mean of the four 'medium' breeds in S9 (Fox Terrier, Teckel, Basset Hound, Beagle); a = adult weight of the target dog.
logistic_model.check: Implied time to 99 percent adult weight = x0 + b*ln(99) = 57.4 weeks, consistent with S9 T99 of 52-58 weeks for the medium breeds.
logistic_model.notes: UNSOURCED — proposal. Neither Border Collie nor mixed breeds were in S9 (21 dogs). Applying the medium-breed shape to them is an assumption. Interpretation of 1/b as % per week is ours; it is consistent with the reported T99. Model is not valid near birth.

percent_of_adult_weight_by_month.notes: UNSOURCED — proposal. Computed from logistic_model (S9 medium-breed shape).

8_12_weeks.quote: Puppies eight to 12 weeks old need four meals a day.
8_12_weeks.notes: RKC (S21): 'From two to three months – four meals a day'. RSPCA AU (S20): 'at least 4 times per day to begin with'.

3_6_months.quote: Feed puppies three to six months old three meals a day.
3_6_months.notes: RKC (S21): 'From four to six months – two to three meals a day'.

6_12_months.quote: Feed puppies six months to one year two meals a day.
6_12_months.notes: RKC (S21): 'Over six months – two meals a day (depending on the breed)'.

adult.quote: The most common recommendation is to feed your dog at least two meals per day.
adult.notes: Sources disagree: ASPCA (S18) 'one meal a day is usually enough' after the first birthday; RSPCA AU (S20) 'adult dogs should be fed at least twice per day to help avoid bloat'. 2 chosen as majority.

senior.quote: feeding your dog smaller meals two or three times a day
senior.notes: AAHA (S13): 'Maintenance energy requirements (MER) generally decrease over a dog's lifetime.'
senior.decision: potrdil David 2026-10-05: senior = 2 meals/day (lower end of 2–3)

hunger_physiology.unit: hours after a meal until hunger signals
hunger_physiology.quote: After 8 to 10 hours, an empty stomach begins to send signals to the brain that stimulate a hunger response.
hunger_physiology.notes: Useful for hunger decay calibration of adults.

daily_requirement.quote: Generally, dogs require 60-80 ml of water per kg of body weight
daily_requirement.notes: FirstVet (S23): normal 'between 20-70ml/kg body weight per day'; abnormal 'more than 100ml/kg'. Sources differ; general only, not by age or breed.

excessive_threshold.quote: more than 100ml/kg body weight per day

availability.quote: Clean, fresh water should be available at all times
availability.notes: RSPCA AU (S20): 'Fresh drinking water must be available at all times'. No source gives a number of refills per day.

refills_per_day.notes: UNSOURCED — proposal. Game abstraction only (current breed_configs value). Real advice is 'water always available'; no source supports a refill count.

puppy_rule_of_thumb.value: 5 min × age in months, twice a day, until full-grown
puppy_rule_of_thumb.quote: five minutes of exercise per month of age, twice a day, until the puppy is full-grown
puppy_rule_of_thumb.notes: CONTESTED: Veterinary Ireland Journal (S25) lists it among 'misconceptions like five minutes of exercise per month of life'. No study behind the number was found.
puppy_rule_of_thumb.decision: potrdil David 2026-10-05: puppy and young dog = 10 min/day × age in months, capped at the adult minutes (rule stays contested, confidence low)

puppy_evidence.value: off-lead exercise on soft ground ≤ 3 months protective; stairs ≤ 3 months risk
puppy_evidence.quote: puppies ≤ 3 months old should not be allowed access to stairs, but should be allowed outdoor exercise on soft ground
puppy_evidence.notes: Only Newfoundland, Labrador, Leonberger, Irish Wolfhound (large/giant).

adult_general.quote: all adult dogs should receive between 30 minutes and two hours of physical activity and mental stimulation daily

senior.value: frequent short walks instead of one long one
senior.quote: try to go for frequent short walks instead of one long one

steps_conversion.unit: human steps per minute of walking
steps_conversion.quote: ≥100 steps/min is a consistent heuristic … associated with absolutely defined moderate intensity (3 metabolic equivalents (METs))
steps_conversion.notes: ASSUMPTION for the game: child's steps = walk minutes × 100. S45 covers ADULTS only ('cadence-based research in children and adolescents is currently less developed'). No veterinary source gives a step goal for dogs (see S46).

measured_16_weeks.quote: mean total hours of sleep in this subpopulation was reported as 11.2 h (SD = 2.9)
measured_16_weeks.notes: Owner-reported cohort (Dogs Trust Generation Pup). Lower than RKC figures — conflict; RKC may include dozing/resting.

senior.value: sleep more; daytime sleep + night restlessness is a sign of cognitive dysfunction
senior.quote: can become less energetic and tend to sleep more
senior.notes: AAHA (S13): 'daytime sleeping and nighttime restlessness' are the most common clinical signs of cognitive dysfunction (DISHAA). No hours given.

hold_bladder.value: 1 hour per month of age (±1 h)
hold_bladder.quote: one hour for each month of age, give or take an hour
hold_bladder.notes: WebMD/DVM-reviewed (S31): '1 hour for every month of age until they're about a year old'.

adult_hold.quote: can reasonably be expected to hold their urine for 8 hours or longer … about every four hours when possible

when_to_go_out.value: after eating, naps, strenuous play, change of activity
when_to_go_out.quote: puppies may need to eliminate after eating, naps, strenuous play, or whenever there is a change of activity

consistent_from.quote: they may not become consistent until they're between 12 and 16 weeks old

fully_trained.quote: It typically takes 4-6 months for a puppy to be fully house trained, but some puppies may take up to a year.

accidents.quote: Accidents are common with puppies up to a year old.
accidents.notes: No accident frequency (per day) found in any source.

daytime_trips_puppy.quote: you can expect to take puppies out every 2 hours or so during the day

learns_to_signal.value: a house-trained puppy can learn to 'ask' to go out (door, bell)
learns_to_signal.quote: Once your puppy is physically mature enough to hold her bladder consistently, she can learn to 'ask' to be taken outside.
learns_to_signal.notes: VCA (S47, E. Lindell VMD DACVB): 'She may develop a signal on her own, such as coming to you and barking, or going to the door and scratching.' Basis of the game effect potty training → fewer accidents (M5-R03); the size of the effect is not sourced.

baby_teeth_in.quote: By now all of your puppy's baby teeth should have come in. Dogs usually have about 28 baby teeth total

baby_teeth_shed.quote: your puppy's baby teeth start to shed (Weeks 12-16)

adult_teeth_in.quote: By the time, your puppy is about six months old or so, all of their puppy teeth should have fallen out, and their adult teeth should have grown in.

intense_chewing_ends.quote: This intensified chewing phase usually ends by six months of age.

destructive_chewing_causes.quote: Bored dogs tend look for ways to entertain themselves, and chewing is one option.

exercise_vs_boredom.value: daily exercise and mental stimulation reduce boredom-driven behaviour
exercise_vs_boredom.quote: Daily exercise and mental stimulation may diminish tendency to seek novelty from boredom

guidance_reduces_chewing.value: guidance / training restricts chewing to appropriate objects
guidance_reduces_chewing.quote: Although puppies do need to chew on things, gentle guidance can teach your puppy to restrict chewing to appropriate objects, like his own toys.
guidance_reduces_chewing.notes: ASPCA (S33), fetched 2026-10-06. Basis of the game effect 'place' training → less chewing (M5-R03); the size of the effect is not sourced.

start_age.quote: Puppies can begin very simple training starting as soon as they come home, usually around 8 weeks old.
start_age.decision: potrdil David 2026-10-05: a puppy arrives at 2 months

session_length_puppy.quote: Always keep training sessions brief — just five to 10 minutes
session_length_puppy.notes: PetMD (S37): 'about five minutes each … no more than 15 minutes per day'.

daily_total_puppy.quote: try to average a total of no more than 15 minutes per day

first_commands.quote: Teach Your Dog to Come When Called, Loose-Leash Walking, Sit, Down, Stay

socialization_window.quote: socialization must happen during the sensitive period (~3 to 14 weeks of age)

adolescent_obedience_dip.quote: a reduction in obedience, during puberty (at around eight months of age)

adult_session_length.notes: UNSOURCED — proposal. No source found for adult session length.

coren_tiers.unit: repetitions to learn a new command / % obeys first command
coren_tiers.quote: Brightest Dogs Understanding of new commands: fewer than 5 repetitions.; Obey first command: 95% of the time or better.
coren_tiers.notes: Secondary source (Wikipedia). Survey of obedience judges, not an experiment; verify in the book before use.

all_dogs_median_uk.quote: On average, companion dogs live for 12.5 years.

medium_breeds_median_uk.quote: medium-sized breeds were found to live longer, with lifespans of 12.5 years

size_effect.quote: increasing bodyweight was negatively correlated with longevity

identity.value: FCI No. 297, Group 1 Section 1, Great Britain
identity.quote: Standard Number: 297; Group 1 - Shepherd and Cattle Dogs; Country of Origin: Great Britain

fci_ideal.quote: Ideal height at withers: Males: 53 cm (21 ins), Females: slightly less.

akc_range.quote: The height at the withers varies from 19 to 22 inches for males, 18 to 21 inches for females.

akc.quote: weigh between 30 and 55 pounds
akc.notes: Neither FCI nor AKC standard gives weight.

pdsa.notes: Conflicts with AKC; heavier than Salt category IV typical. Prefer AKC.

salt_category.value: IV (15–<30 kg) — by AKC weight it spans III/IV
salt_category.notes: Border Collie itself was not in the Salt dataset; category assignment by weight is ours.

adult_weight_reached.notes: Size-class value, not breed-specific.

weight_by_month_kg.notes: UNSOURCED — proposal. = AKC adult range × logistic % (general_by_size.growth.logistic_model).

median_uk.notes: S16 confirms x̃ = 13.1.

senior_from.notes: Derived: AAHA senior = last 25% of lifespan (S11) × median 13.1 y (S15) → 0.75 × 13.1 = 9.8 y. Dogs Trust rule of thumb says > 7 y (S14).
senior_from.decision: potrdil David 2026-10-05: senior from 118 months (0.75 × 13.1 y)

adult.quote: Exercise: More than 2 hours per day
adult.notes: PDSA (S7): 'a minimum of two hours exercise every day'.

energy.value: very high energy
energy.quote: a very high energy breed

temperament.value: tenacious, hard-working, great tractability; keen, alert, responsive, intelligent; neither nervous nor aggressive
temperament.quote: Tenacious, hard-working, of great tractability. Keen, alert, responsive and intelligent. Neither nervous nor aggressive.

boredom_chewing.quote: If left alone or not given enough exercise, your Collie will certainly let you know they're unhappy by chewing anything in paw's reach!

herding_children.quote: natural herding instincts may lead them to herd children during play

mental_stimulation.quote: always need to have something to do, so making sure they have mental stimulation is very important

coren_rank.quote: 190 of the 199 judges ranked the Border Collie in the top 10
coren_rank.notes: Rank 1 of 130+ breeds (S35). Coren: measures 'working and obedience intelligence' only.

coren_tier.quote: Brightest Dogs … fewer than 5 repetitions … 95% of the time or better
coren_tier.notes: Tier definitions from Wikipedia; verify in book.

genetic_biddability.value: Border Collie ancestry associated with higher biddability
genetic_biddability.quote: border collie ancestry correlates with increased biddability
genetic_biddability.notes: But breed explains ~9% of individual behaviour variation (S42) — individual dogs vary.

learning_multiplier.notes: UNSOURCED as a number — game value. Coren ranks the Border Collie #1 (S34) and puts it in the 'brightest' tier (<5 repetitions to learn a command vs 25–40 for 'average', S35 — secondary source), but gives no speed factor. Training progress per correctly timed praise × 2.
learning_multiplier.decision: potrdil David 2026-10-06: Border Collie learns ~2× faster than the mixed-breed baseline (M5-R03)

general.value: well proportioned, smooth outline, sufficient substance for endurance
general.quote: Well proportioned, smooth outline showing quality, gracefulness and perfect balance, combined with sufficient substance to give impression of endurance.

coat_varieties.quote: Two varieties: Moderately long or Smooth. In both, topcoat dense and medium textured, undercoat soft and dense
coat_varieties.notes: AKC (S3) also two varieties, double coat.

colour_rule.value: any colour; white must never predominate (FCI/UK); AKC: all colours/combinations equal
colour_rule.quote: Variety of colours permissible. White should never predominate.
colour_rule.notes: AKC (S3): 'appears in all colors or combination of colors and/or markings. All colors are to be judged equally'. No standard lists specific colours or their frequencies.

colour_list_and_weights.notes: UNSOURCED — proposal. Specific colour names (black & white, tricolour, red, blue, merles, sable) and their frequencies are NOT in FCI/AKC/UK standards. The AKC breed page colour list could not be accessed. Draft weights in breed_appearance.php are unsourced.

ears.quote: Carried erect or semi-erect and sensitive in use.
ears.notes: AKC (S3): 'one or both carried erect and/or semi-erect' → supports mixed carriage.

eyes.value: brown; in merles one or both, or part of one or both, may be blue
eyes.quote: Brown in colour except in merles where one or both or part of one or both may be blue.
eyes.notes: RKC (S6) identical. AKC (S3): 'Any eye color is acceptable, but blue eyes in dogs other than merle are not preferred.' Amber is not named by any standard.

tail.value: moderately long, low set, upward swirl towards end
tail.quote: Moderately long, the bone reaching at least to hock, set on low, well-furnished and with an upward swirl towards the end.

face_markings.notes: UNSOURCED — proposal. No standard describes blaze / face markings. Draft 'markings' list is unsourced.

labrador_retriever._note: Added 2026-10-09 (M5-R10-01). Quotes as returned by the web-fetch tool on 2026-10-09; spot-check before import (sources.md S48–S62).

identity.value: FCI No. 122, Group 8 Section 1 (Retrievers), Great Britain
identity.quote: Standard number: 122; Group n°8 - Chiens rapporteurs de gibier - Chiens leveurs de gibier - Chiens d'eau; Section: Rapporteurs de gibier; Country of origin: GRANDE-BRETAGNE
identity.notes: FCI standard (S48): 'Group 8 Retrievers, Flushing dogs, Water dogs. Section 1 Retrievers.' 'UTILIZATION: Retriever.' Definitive FCI acceptance 24/12/1954 (S49). NOTE: both S48 and S49 give 'DATE OF PUBLICATION OF THE OFFICIAL VALID STANDARD: 08.09.2026' (EN version dated 06.10.2026) — a very recent revision; verify on fci.be.

size_class.notes: PDSA (S53): 'Size: Large'. Woodgreen (S60): 'Size: Large'. AKC breed page (S62) calls it a 'medium-to-large dog'.

fci_ideal.quote: Ideal height at the withers: Males: 56 – 57 cm. Females: 54 – 56 cm.
fci_ideal.notes: RKC standard (S51) differs for bitches: 'Ideal height at withers: dogs: 56-57 cms (22-22½ ins); bitches: 55-56 cms (21½-22 ins).' PDSA (S53): 'Height: 55-57 cm'.

rkc_ideal.quote: Ideal height at withers: dogs: 56-57 cms (22-22½ ins); bitches: 55-56 cms (21½-22 ins).
rkc_ideal.notes: Bitch lower limit 55 cm vs FCI 54 cm (S48).

akc_range.quote: The height at the withers for a dog is 22½ to 24½ inches; for a bitch is 21½ to 23½ inches.
akc_range.notes: AKC allows taller dogs than FCI/RKC (up to 62.2 cm vs 57 cm).

akc.unit: kg (converted from dogs 65–80 lb, bitches 55–70 lb)
akc.quote: Approximate weight of dogs and bitches in working condition: dogs 65 to 80 pounds; bitches 55 to 70 pounds.
akc.notes: From the AKC breed standard (approved 1994). Overall 24.9–36.3 kg. FCI (S48) and RKC (S51) standards give no weight.

pdsa.notes: Woodgreen (S60): 'Weight: 25-36 kg'. Consistent with AKC.

uk_measured_mean.quote: The mean adult bodyweight of males (35.2 kg, SD 5.9 kg) was higher than for females (30.4 kg, SD 5.2 kg) (P < 0.001).
uk_measured_mean.notes: Measured in UK primary-care Labradors (VetCompass, McGreevy et al. 2018). Males average at the top of the AKC range; note 8.8 % were recorded overweight/obese.

salt_category.value: V (30–<40 kg) by measured UK means; AKC range spans IV/V
salt_category.quote: Category IV: 15 to <30 kg; Category V: 30 to <40 kg
salt_category.notes: Category assignment by weight is ours; whether Salt 2017 listed the Labrador in a category could not be checked (PMC not reachable 2026-10-09).

adult_weight_reached.notes: Size-class value, not breed-specific. Labrador AKC males 65–80 lb are 'Large'; bitches 55–70 lb straddle Medium (24–59 lb: 12–15 months) and Large. Salt (S8): 'larger breeds requiring up to 24 months to reach adult body weight'. Quote is a table row on the page (Large (59–99 pounds) | 15–18 months).

weight_by_month_kg.notes: UNSOURCED — proposal. Not derived: the existing logistic shape (general_by_size.growth.logistic_model) is a MEDIUM-breed curve (≈99 % at 57 weeks) and would contradict the large-breed 15–18 months (S10). A large-breed curve needs a source (S9 has no large breed; Salt 2017 raw data not downloadable). Open question for David.

median_uk.notes: McMillan et al. 2024 (Sci Rep), corrected Figure 3 legend (author correction, same document as S16, read from the LJMU repository copy because PMC was not reachable). The Dogs Trust summary page (S15) does not list the Labrador. Conflicts with S55 (12.0 y).

median_uk_vetcompass_2018.quote: The median longevity of Labrador retrievers overall was 12.0 years (IQR 9.9–13.8, range 0.0–16.0).
median_uk_vetcompass_2018.notes: McGreevy, Wilson, …, O'Neill (2018) — VetCompass, 33,320 Labradors under care in 2013; longevity from the deaths in a random sample. Colour effect: 'The median longevity of non-chocolate coloured dogs (n = 139, 12.1 years…' vs '…chocolate coloured animals (n = 34, 10.7 years…' (S55; press summary S56).

rkc.notes: PDSA (S53): 'Over 10 years'. Woodgreen (S60): 'Life expectancy: 10-12 years'.

senior_from.notes: Derived: AAHA senior = last 25% of lifespan (S11) × median 13.1 y (S54) → 0.75 × 13.1 = 9.8 y = 118 months (same as Border Collie). With the VetCompass median 12.0 y (S55): 0.75 × 12.0 = 9.0 y = 108 months. Dogs Trust rule of thumb > 7 y (S14).

adult.quote: Exercise: More than 2 hours per day
adult.notes: Sources disagree: Guide Dogs UK (S59): 'Labrador retrievers generally need at least 90 minutes of exercise daily as adults.'; Woodgreen (S60): 'Exercise needs: 60-90 mins'; PDSA (S53) gives no minutes: 'Full of energy, Labradors need a lot of exercise and mental enrichment each day to keep them physically fit'. Confidence lowered to medium for the conflict.

energy.value: full of energy, very active
energy.quote: Full of energy, Labradors need a lot of exercise and mental enrichment each day to keep them physically fit
energy.notes: FCI (S48): 'Strongly built, short-coupled, very active'.

temperament.value: good-tempered, very agile; intelligent, keen and biddable, strong will to please; kindly, no aggression or undue shyness; adaptable, devoted companion
temperament.quote: Good-tempered, very agile. Excellent nose, soft mouth; keen lover of water. Adaptable, devoted companion. Intelligent, keen and biddable, with a strong will to please. Kindly nature, with no trace of aggression or undue shyness.
temperament.notes: Returned by the tool in three consecutive fragments; RKC (S51) same wording ('keen love of water'). AKC (S52): 'The ideal disposition is one of a kindly, outgoing, tractable nature;' 'eager to please and non-aggressive towards man or animal.'

food_motivation.quote: They're generally described as intelligent, enjoy learning, and highly food motivated
food_motivation.notes: Cambridge (S58): 'People who live with Labradors often say they are obsessed by food.' S55: 'They are often of stocky build with a tendency to eat beyond their physiological needs...'. Genetic basis: S57.

pomc_deletion.value: POMC gene deletion associated with higher body weight and greater food motivation; ~23 % of Labradors carry ≥1 copy
pomc_deletion.quote: The deletion … associated with body weight (per allele effect of 0.33 SD) … greater food motivation; allele frequency of 12%
pomc_deletion.notes: Raffan et al. 2016, Cell Metab 23:893–900 (abstract fragments as returned; ellipses ours). Press release (S58): 'Around one in four (23%) Labradors is thought to carry at least one copy of the variant.' and 'for each copy of the gene carried, the dog was on average 1.9kg heavier.'

obesity_tendency.value: prone to obesity; 8.8 % recorded overweight/obese in UK primary care
obesity_tendency.notes: S55: 'overweight/obesity (183, 8.8%, 95% CI: 7.6–10.1)' — 2nd most common disorder after otitis externa (10.4 %). S56: 'We found that 8.8 percent of UK Labradors are overweight or obese.'

chewing.value: retrievers chew a lot through adolescence (to ~2 years)
chewing.quote: Retrievers, especially, are known for their love of chewing throughout their adolescence
chewing.notes: Single tier-C source (vet column, 2012); the saying 'Chew till they're two; shed till they're dead.' is folklore, not data. Same page attributes it to the retrieving instinct and too little exercise. No tier A/B Labrador-specific chewing source found.

family.value: bonds with the whole family; good family pet with socialisation
family.quote: They usually bond well with the whole family and are affectionate and loving.
family.notes: PDSA (S53): 'Labradors make perfect family pets, given the right socialisation, as with all breeds.'

coren_rank.notes: Rank 7 in Coren's list as reproduced on Wikipedia (table row). Coren's own article (S34) could not be fetched on 2026-10-09 — verify in the book. Top 10: Border Collie, Poodle, German Shepherd, Golden Retriever, Doberman, Shetland Sheepdog, Labrador, Papillon, Rottweiler, Australian Cattle Dog.

coren_tier.quote: Understanding of new commands: fewer than 5 repetitions.; Obey first command: 95% of the time or better.;
coren_tier.notes: Same tier as the Border Collie (ranks 1–10). Tier definitions from Wikipedia; verify in book.

training_notes.value: obedient, quick to learn, eager to please; treats work well
training_notes.quote: They're obedient, quick to learn and eager to please.
training_notes.notes: Guide Dogs UK (S59): 'With their known famed love of food, Labradors may enjoy treats as part of training and food-based games and puzzles.' Woodgreen (S60): 'Training: Moderately easy'.

learning_multiplier.notes: UNSOURCED — proposal — see proposed_game_parameters.labrador_retriever.learning_multiplier (needs David's decision).

general.value: strongly built, short-coupled, very active; broad skull; broad, deep chest
general.quote: Strongly built, short-coupled, very active; broad in skull; broad and deep through chest and ribs; broad and strong over loins and hindquarters.
general.notes: RKC (S51) adds that agility 'precludes excessive body weight or excessive substance'.

colours.quote: Wholly black, yellow or liver/chocolate. Yellows range from light cream to fox red, livers/chocolates range from light to dark.
colours.notes: Solid colours only: 'Small white spot on chest and the rear of pasterns permissible.' 'Any other colour or combination of colours unacceptable.' RKC (S51): 'The only correct colours are wholly black, yellow and liver/chocolate.' AKC (S52): 'The Labrador Retriever coat colors are black, yellow and chocolate.' Colour frequencies: not sourced.

colour_weights.notes: UNSOURCED — proposal. No source gives colour frequencies. Note for game: chocolate Labradors had a shorter median life (10.7 vs 12.1 y, S55) — do not model unless David wants it.

coat.value: short, dense, no wave or feathering, fairly hard to the touch; weather-resistant undercoat
coat.quote: Distinctive feature, short, dense, without wave or feathering, giving fairly hard feel to the touch; weather-resistant undercoat.
coat.notes: AKC (S52): 'It should be short, straight and very dense, giving a fairly hard feeling to the hand.' RKC (S50): 'Coat length: Short'.

tail.value: 'otter' tail: very thick at base, tapering, medium length, no feathering; not curled over back
tail.quote: Distinctive feature, very thick towards base, gradually tapering towards tip, medium length, free from feathering, but clothed thickly all round with short, thick, dense coat, thus giving "rounded" appearance described as "Otter" tail. May be carried gaily, but should not curl over back.
tail.notes: Returned in four consecutive fragments; RKC (S51) identical.

The Golden is NOT in the corrected Fig. 3 legend (S54 checked 2026-10-09); the full paper (nature.com) was not reachable — verify the 13.2 in its supplementary table. Conflicts with S71 (12.48 y).

health._note: Parent-facing background only. Brachycephaly is the breed's defining welfare issue and every source on the breed raises it; recorded factually with sources, no invented percentages. Percentages below come from clinic records or a self-selected testing scheme — each carries its context; do not show any of them to children. Breathing/heat are proposed as a gentle game mechanic (proposed_game_parameters.french_bulldog.heat_breathing_mechanic), not as statistics.

brachycephaly_boas.value: flat-faced (brachycephalic) breed; at risk of brachycephalic obstructive airway syndrome (BOAS) — narrow nostrils, excess soft tissue, noisy/laboured breathing
brachycephaly_boas.quote: The soft tissue in the nose and throat of some brachycephalic dogs may be excessive for the airways
brachycephaly_boas.notes: RKC breed page (S78) also: 'Some dogs may also have narrow nostrils making it even more difficult to breathe.'; 'dogs with a very flat face and short muzzle have a higher risk of developing certain health issues'; 'Not all flat-faced dogs will have the health issues described'. PDSA (S81): 'Frenchies are a flat-faced breed, which can often cause breathing problems.'; BOAS 'can cause severe breathing problems and is caused by their shorter faces.' Woodgreen (S82): 'Unfortunately, Frenchies are prone to several health conditions including breathing problems'. Cambridge (S90): BOAS is 'a progressive disorder that can impair a dog's ability to exercise, play, eat and sleep'. Standards: FCI (S76) 'The slope of the nostrils as well as the upturned nose must, however, allow normal nasal breathing.' — disqualifying faults 'Respiratory distress.' and 'Completely closed nostrils.'; RKC (S79) 'Dogs showing respiratory distress or making excessive respiratory noise unacceptable.'

boas_odds_vs_other_dogs.unit: odds ratio vs non-French Bulldogs (UK primary care, 2016)
boas_odds_vs_other_dogs.notes: O'Neill et al. 2021 (S84), 2,781 French Bulldogs vs 21,850 other dogs: BOAS OR 30.89; stenotic nares '(OR 42.14; 95 % CI 18.50 to 95.99; p < 0.001)'; also aural discharge OR 14.40, skin fold dermatitis OR 11.18, dystocia OR 9.13. Increased odds for '20/43 (46.5 %) disorders', reduced for '11/43 (25.6 %)'. Conclusion: 'the health of French Bulldogs has diverged substantially from, and may be lower than,' [the rest of the dog population — completion paraphrased]; 'Many of these predispositions are closely associated with the conformational extremes that define the French Bulldog breed.' Odds ratios = relative risk of a vet recording the diagnosis, NOT the share of Frenchies affected.

boas_diagnosed_prevalence_2013.unit: % of French Bulldogs with a recorded BOAS diagnosis in one year (2013)
boas_diagnosed_prevalence_2013.notes: O'Neill et al. 2018 (S83), 2,228 French Bulldogs, median age 1.3 y. A one-year recorded-diagnosis rate in a very young population — the paper notes older dogs were significantly more likely to have a BOAS diagnosis (paraphrase), so it understates lifetime risk. Do NOT present as 'only 2.4 % are affected'.

rfg_grades_2024.unit: % of French Bulldogs graded in the RKC/Cambridge Respiratory Function Grading scheme (cumulative to 31/12/2024)
rfg_grades_2024.notes: Row of the RKC annual RFG report 2024 (S89); column headers were garbled and matched to Grade 0–3 by position by the tool (counts sum to 1,831; 301 tested in 2024). Self-selected population (mostly dogs of health-testing breeders) — NOT representative of pet Frenchies. Scheme (S90): grade 0–3 after an exercise tolerance test; 'dogs graded as three will show severe respiratory signs of BOAS'; 'The scheme issues guidance that dogs graded three should not be bred from.' Grade definitions 0–2 not returned.

heat_stroke.value: higher risk of heat-related illness; brachycephalic dogs OR 2.10 vs mesocephalic; French Bulldog about 6× (odds vs Labrador, press summary)
heat_stroke.quote: Brachycephalic dogs had higher odds of HRI (OR 2.10, 95% CI 1.68-2.64) compared to mesocephalic dogs.
heat_stroke.notes: Hall, Carter & O'Neill 2020 (S86), 905,543 UK dogs (2016), 395 confirmed events, incidence '0.04% (95% CI 0.04-0.05%)', event fatality '14.18% (95% CI 11.08 – 17.96%)'. French Bulldog vs Labrador: the fetched text says significantly higher odds but did not return the OR; RVC VetCompass news (S87): 'French Bulldog (x6)' compared with Labradors; NTU press release (S88): 'flat-faced dogs in general were twice as likely'. Verify the exact French Bulldog OR in the paper's table. PDSA (S81) and Woodgreen (S82): 'Frenchies are also more vulnerable to heat stroke than other breeds'. BVA (S91): breathing difficulties are 'often associated with overheating'.

other_conditions.value: skin-fold dermatitis, ear disease (otitis), eye problems, spinal/intervertebral disc disease, luxating patellas, dental problems, dystocia
other_conditions.notes: O'Neill 2018 (S83) most common recorded disorders 2013 (tool listed: otitis externa 14.0 %, diarrhoea 7.5 %, conjunctivitis 3.2 %, overlong nails 3.1 %, skin fold dermatitis 3.0 % — quote assembled from that list). PDSA (S81) lists luxating patellas, dental problems, eye problems incl. cataracts, intervertebral disc disease, skin fold dermatitis, hyperuricosuria (list summarised by the tool) and: 'it's important to make sure their skin folds are kept clean and dry.' RKC (S78): skin folds 'can make a warm, moist environment which is perfect for bacteria and yeast to grow'; 'Some brachycephalic dogs may have shallow eye sockets, causing their eyes to become more prominent'. Woodgreen (S82): 'All this can be very expensive to treat.'

merle_colour.value: merle is not a breed-standard colour and carries a hearing/sight risk
merle_colour.quote: the merle gene in this breed carries an increased risk of impaired hearing and sight problems
merle_colour.notes: RKC lists merle-type/blue/black-and-tan etc. as non-breed-standard (NBS) colours (S78); FCI (S76) and AKC (S80) also exclude them. Game should not offer merle/blue Frenchies (see appearance.colours).

welfare_advice_to_buyers.value: UK vets/welfare groups urge people to stop and think before buying a flat-faced dog; PDSA recommends considering a different breed, a cross-breed, or adopting an adult
welfare_advice_to_buyers.quote: We'd recommend considering a different breed or a cross-breed to try and reduce some of the problems Frenchies have.
welfare_advice_to_buyers.notes: PDSA (S81) also: 'Adopting an adult French Bulldog from a rescue centre may be a more cost-effective option.'; if buying, an Assured Breeder with health-screened parents (paraphrase). UK Brachycephalic Working Group (S93): 'Stop and think before buying a flat-faced dog.' (also Science for Animal Welfare / UFAW S94, which names French Bulldogs, Pugs and Bulldogs, and O'Neill in S87). Woodgreen (S82): 'Due to their poor hereditary health, it's essential to buy a French Bulldog from a respectable breeder'. RVC (S85, O'Neill): the research 'may also assist potential new owners to decide whether a French Bulldog is even the right breed for them.' BVA (S91, policy position January 2018): a '3104% increase in French Bulldog registrations'; BVA exec summary (S92): 'increasing awareness of the health and welfare issues associated with brachycephaly amongst current and prospective owners' and 'avoiding imagery of brachycephalic dogs in advertising, marketing materials and social media campaigns' — David 2026-10-10: no French Bulldog imagery in PetPrep marketing / store screenshots (proposed_game_parameters.french_bulldog.marketing). No source found that says vets advise against owning a Frenchie outright; the wording is 'stop and think' / 'consider a different breed'.

coren_rank.notes: Wikipedia table (S35, tier C), between Pug (57) and Griffon Bruxellois/Maltese (59). Coren's own article (S34) lists only the top and bottom 10 — the French Bulldog is in neither (the 'Bulldog' in its bottom 10 is the English Bulldog). Verify in The Intelligence of Dogs.

coren_tier.quote: Understanding of new commands: 40 to 80 repetitions.; Obey first command: 30% of the time or better.
coren_tier.notes: Tier 'Fair Working/Obedience Intelligence' = ranks 55–69 — one tier below 'Average' (ranks 40–54: 25–40 repetitions, ≥50 %). Tier definitions from Wikipedia; verify in book.

training_notes.value: eager to please but can be strong-willed; sensitive — reward-based training
training_notes.quote: French Bulldogs are eager to please their owners which can make them easy to train
training_notes.notes: Sentence continues 'but are also known to be strong-willed at times.' PDSA: 'They are a sensitive breed, so respond best to positive, reward-based training.'; for first-time owners: 'we'd recommend taking them to accredited training classes.' Woodgreen (S82): 'Training: Moderately easy' (same as Labrador/Golden). Sources are milder than Coren's rank.

learning_multiplier.notes: Game value — see proposed_game_parameters.french_bulldog.learning_multiplier (0.7, potrdil David 2026-10-10).

general.value: small molossian; powerful for its size, short, stocky, compact, smooth-coated
general.quote: A powerful dog for its small size, short, stocky, compact in all its proportions, smooth-coated,
general.notes: RKC (S79): 'Sturdy, compact , solid, small dog with good bone, short, smooth coat. No point exaggerated, balance essential.'

colours.quote: The only correct colours are: Brindle; Fawn; Pied;
colours.notes: RKC standard (S79) also: 'Any other colour or combination of colours unacceptable.' FCI (S76): 'fawn, brindled or not, with or without white spotting.' RKC breed page (S78) standard colours: Brindle, Light Brindle, Dark Brindle, Brindle & White, Fawn, Fawn & White, Fawn Pied, Fawn With Black Mask, Pied; non-breed-standard: blue, black & tan, brown, sable, red, cream variants (merle health risk — health.merle_colour). AKC (S80): 'Acceptable colors: white, cream, fawn (ranging from light fawn to a red fawn), or any combinations of the foregoing.' (AKC markings list not returned). Frequencies: not sourced.

colour_weights.notes: UNSOURCED — game draft (verified=false in breed_appearance.php). No colour frequencies. Draw over the standard colours fawn / brindle / pied (RKC S79, FCI S76); fawn weighted highest so the register portrait is fawn (David 2026-10-10); never blue / merle / black-and-tan (S78).

coat.value: smooth, close, glossy, soft, no undercoat
coat.quote: Smooth coat, close, glossy and soft, without undercoat.
coat.notes: RKC (S79): 'Texture fine, smooth, lustrous, short and close.' AKC (S80): 'Coat is brilliant, short and smooth.' RKC breed page (S78): 'Coat length: Short'.

ears.value: bat ears — erect, wide at base, rounded top
ears.quote: ’Bat ears‘, of medium size, wide at base, rounded at top; set high, carried upright and parallel
ears.notes: FCI (S76): 'Set high on the head, but not too close together, carried erect.' AKC (S80): 'Known as the bat ear, broad at the base, elongated, with round top, set high on the head but not too close together'. One ear type → no variation.

eyes.value: dark, round, moderate size
eyes.quote: Preferably dark and matching. Moderate size, round, neither sunken nor prominent
eyes.notes: AKC (S80): 'Eyes dark, brown or approaching black in color, wide apart, set low down in the skull' (blue/green disqualified — paraphrase).

tail.value: naturally short, low-set, straight or screwed
tail.quote: Undocked, set low, thick at root, tapering quickly towards tip, preferably straight, and long enough to cover anus.
tail.notes: FCI (S76): 'Naturally short, ideally long enough to cover the anus, set low,'. AKC (S80): 'The tail is either straight or screwed (but not curly), short, hung low, thick root and fine tip;'.

nose.value: black, broad, short with open nostrils
nose.quote: Nose black and wide, relatively short, with visibly open nostrils and line between well defined.
nose.notes: FCI (S76): 'Black, broad, snubbed, with symmetrical and well opened nostrils, slanting towards the rear.' For PetPrep art: draw visibly open nostrils and a moderate (not extreme) face — RKC 'No point exaggerated' (S79); David 2026-10-10: moderate face with open nostrils in the app art; no Frenchie imagery in marketing (BVA S92, proposed_game_parameters.french_bulldog.marketing).

suitability._note: AKC breed-trait ratings not attempted (the AKC breed pages returned no trait data for the Labrador/Golden). Source = RKC breed-page fields (S78), PDSA (S81), Woodgreen (S82) — same approach as the Labrador/Golden.

rkc_exercise.quote: Exercise: Up to 1 hour per day

rkc_size_of_home.notes: Only breed so far with 'Flat/ Apartment' (Labrador/Golden: 'Large house').

rkc_size_of_garden.quote: Size of garden: Small/ medium garden

rkc_grooming.notes: PDSA (S81): weekly brush; skin folds must be kept clean and dry.

rkc_shedding.notes: Conflict: PDSA (S81) 'French Bulldogs aren't known for shedding lots'; Woodgreen (S82) 'Shedding: Minimal'. → neither `sheds` nor `low_shedding` proposed.

rkc_good_with_children.notes: The RKC breed page shows no 'Good with children' field (as returned 2026-10-10).

pdsa_family.value: popular family pet
pdsa_family.quote: Frenchies are known for being pretty laid back and adaptable, so they tend to get along well with children of all ages
pdsa_family.notes: Continues 'which makes them popular family pets.' (returned as a continuation, over the tool's quote length).

pdsa_children.value: get along well with children of all ages (supervise play)
pdsa_children.quote: Frenchies are known for being pretty laid back and adaptable, so they tend to get along well with children of all ages
pdsa_children.notes: A statement, not a rating; PDSA advises supervising play (paraphrase). Woodgreen (S82): 'tolerant of children'.

pdsa_first_time_owner.value: training classes recommended for first-time owners
pdsa_first_time_owner.quote: If you're a first time owner, we'd recommend taking them to accredited training classes.
pdsa_first_time_owner.notes: Not a 'good first dog' statement (contrast Golden S68) → no first_time_owner tag.

pdsa_time_alone.value: could develop separation anxiety if left alone; never more than 4 h (generic)
pdsa_time_alone.quote: They thrive off company and so could develop separation anxiety if left alone.

woodgreen_sociable_with_pets.notes: PDSA (S81): 'French Bulldogs do have a high prey drive.'

pdsa_monthly_cost.notes: Label and value returned separately by the tool and assembled here. UK prices. Woodgreen (S82): health problems 'can be very expensive to treat.'

german_shepherd._note: Added 2026-10-10 (M5-R10-04, unattended run). Quotes as returned by the web-fetch tool on 2026-10-10; spot-check before import (sources.md S95–S102, reused S8, S10, S11, S14, S24, S34, S45). Pages were partly returned as paraphrase — only passages the tool returned in quotation marks are used as quotes. McMillan 2024 (S54) and the Dogs Trust summary (S15) were not reachable in this run (permission request withdrawn), so the lifespan is the VetCompass breed median (S101) per the runbook rule. Woodgreen and the AKC standard page could not be fetched.

identity.value: FCI No. 166, Group 1 Section 1 (Sheepdogs), Germany
identity.quote: Group: n°1 - Sheepdogs and Cattledogs (except Swiss Cattledogs); Section: Sheepdogs; Country of origin: GERMANY
identity.notes: FCI nomenclature (S96): standard number 166; 'Subject to a working trial according to the FCI Breeds Nomenclature'; definitive acceptance '1/1/1955'; publication of valid standard '8/11/2010' (the standard PDF S95 was returned as '11.08.2010' — same date, different notation); varieties 'a) Double coat' and 'b) Long and harsh outer coat'. Quote assembled from the nomenclature fields.

size_class.notes: PDSA (S100): 'Size: Large'. FCI (S95) calls the dog 'medium-size' in the general appearance, but its weights (♂ 30–40 kg, ♀ 22–32 kg) and the UK sources put it in the large class.

fci_range.quote: Males: Height at the withers: 60 cm to 65 cm; Females: Height at the withers: 55 cm to 60 cm
fci_range.notes: Returned as two fragments ('Height at the withers: 60 cm to 65 cm' for males, '55 cm to 60 cm' for females), assembled here.

rkc_ideal.quote: Ideal height (from withers and just touching elbows): dogs: 63 cms (25 ins); bitches: 58 cms (23 ins).
rkc_ideal.notes: RKC breed standard (last updated 1 August 2025). No weight in the RKC standard.

pdsa_average.notes: PDSA key-facts box (label wording as returned by the tool).

fci.quote: Males: Weight: 30 kg to 40 kg; Females: Weight: 22 kg to 32 kg
fci.notes: Returned as two fragments under the male / female size paragraphs, assembled here. RKC standard (S98) gives no weight; AKC standard not reachable.

pdsa.notes: PDSA key-facts box (label wording as returned by the tool). Heavier than the FCI range.

uk_measured_median.quote: The median adult bodyweight of males (40.1 kg
uk_measured_median.notes: O'Neill et al. 2017 (S101), VetCompass UK primary-care records; females '(34.8 kg, IQR 30.6–39.5, range 15.0–74.0)'. Both medians sit at or above the FCI upper bounds.

salt_category.value: V (30–<40 kg) for males; females span IV/V
salt_category.notes: Category assignment by weight is ours (same method as the Labrador): FCI ♂ 30–40 kg = Category V, ♀ 22–32 kg = IV (15–<30) / V; band limits from general_by_size.size_classes.salt_2017_bands_kg (S8). Salt 2017 breed list not checked.

adult_weight_reached.notes: Size-class value (PetMD S10), not breed-specific. FCI males 30–40 kg (66–88 lb) are 'Large'; females 22–32 kg (48.5–70.5 lb) straddle Medium (24–59 lb: 12–15 months) and Large — same situation as the Labrador, so the same 15–18 months. Salt (S8): 'larger breeds requiring up to 24 months to reach adult body weight'.

weight_by_month_kg.notes: UNSOURCED — no German Shepherd growth curve found; S9 has no large breed (open question shared with the Labrador/Golden).

median_uk.quote: The median longevity of GSDs overall was 10.3 years
median_uk.notes: O'Neill et al. 2017 (S101): IQR 8.0–12.1, range 0.2–17.0, 12,146 GSDs in VetCompass. RVC news (S102): 'The median longevity of GSDs was 10.3 years (IQR 8.0–12.1).' McMillan 2024 (S54) / Dogs Trust (S15) not reachable in this run — runbook rule: else a VetCompass median. Shorter than the Border Collie / Labrador (13.1) and Golden (13.2), longer than the French Bulldog (9.8).

rkc.notes: PDSA (S100): 'Average lifespan: over 10 years' (key-facts label as returned). Consistent with the 10.3 y median (S101).

senior_from.notes: Derived: AAHA senior = last 25 % of lifespan (S11) × 10.3 y (S101) → 0.75 × 10.3 = 7.725 y = 92.7 → 93 months. With the breed-page 'over 10 years' (S97): 0.75 × 10 = 7.5 y = 90 months. Dogs Trust rule of thumb > 7 y = 84 months (S14).

adult.quote: Exercise: More than 2 hours per day
adult.notes: PDSA (S100): 'Your German Shepherd will need a minimum of two hours of exercise every day.' and 'Our vets recommend spreading exercise across the day rather than trying to do two hours all in one go.' (key-facts label 'Minimum exercise: 2 hours per day'). Sources agree: at least 2 h.

energy.value: tireless working dog
energy.quote: Attentive, alert, resilient and tireless with keen scenting ability.
energy.notes: RKC standard characteristics (S98): 'Versatile working dog, balanced and free from exaggeration.' RKC breed page (S97): 'Versatile worker and service dog noted for bravery and intelligence'.

temperament.value: steady, loyal, self-assured, courageous, tractable
temperament.quote: Steady of nerve, loyal, self-assured, courageous and tractable. Never nervous, over-aggressive or shy.
temperament.notes: FCI (S95): the dog 'must be well-balanced (with strong nerves) in terms of character, self-assured, absolutely natural.' RKC Breed Watch (S99) lists 'Nervous temperament' as a point of concern. PDSA (S100): a strong guarding instinct means 'careful training and socialisation will be needed.'

family.value: some make great family pets with children of all ages; always supervise around young children; strong
family.quote: Some can make great family pets in homes with children of all ages
family.notes: PDSA (S100) also: 'dogs should always be supervised around young children' and they 'often don't know their own strength' (around young children or adults unfamiliar with the breed). Hedged ('some can') and with a supervision caveat → family_pet only, not children / small_children.

time_alone.value: thrives on company; worries if left too long
time_alone.quote: thrive on company and will worry about you if you leave them too long
time_alone.notes: PDSA generic rule: 'You should never leave any dog alone for longer than four hours.' → no often_alone tag.

other_pets.value: usually fine with pets they grew up with; may chase unfamiliar cats / small pets
other_pets.quote: usually fine with other family pets they have grown up with
other_pets.notes: PDSA: dogs that did not grow up with cats or small pets may chase them (paraphrase) → conditional, no other_pets tag.

boredom_chewing.value: exercise prevents boredom barking and chewing furniture
boredom_chewing.quote: out of boredom or having a nibble on the furniture
boredom_chewing.notes: PDSA (S100): enough exercise stops dogs barking 'out of boredom or having a nibble on the furniture' (fragment as returned; lead-in paraphrased).

food_motivation.notes: No German Shepherd-specific food-motivation statement found. PDSA (S100) only generic feeding advice ('We usually recommend splitting their daily allowance into two meals.'; treats ≤ 10 % of calories) → no food_motivated_weight tag.

guarding.value: strong guarding instinct — careful training and socialisation
guarding.quote: careful training and socialisation will be needed
guarding.notes: PDSA (S100), context: a strong guarding instinct (paraphrase of the lead-in).

health._note: Parent-facing background only, recorded factually with sources; percentages stay here and are never shown in the app, the register export or audience docs. The conformation concern (hind legs / hips) is the breed's welfare topic in UK sources — RKC Breed Watch (S99), RKC breed page (S97), PDSA (S100), VetCompass (S101).

hind_conformation.value: hind-leg conformation and rear movement are a recognised welfare concern in the breed
hind_conformation.quote: Incorrect hind conformation and/or poor rear movement
hind_conformation.notes: RKC Breed Watch point of concern (S99; page heading 'Category 2', page title says 'Category 3' — as returned); second point 'Nervous temperament'. RKC breed page (S97): 'This breed can be affected by conformational concerns, more information can be found here.' RKC standard (S98): 'Any tendency towards over-angulation of hindquarters, weak hocks, cow hocks or sickle hocks, highly undesirable.' and 'Absolute soundness is essential.' PDSA (S100) says the Kennel Club classes the breed in 'Category Three' because of conformation changes, mostly 'the shape of their back legs and hips' (older wording than the RKC page). O'Neill 2017 (S101): show selection changed conformation toward features 'such as a sloping croup'; 'selective breeding towards lower hindquarters could also increase the probability' of osteoarthritic conditions.

hip_elbow_dysplasia.value: hip and elbow dysplasia — RKC good-practice tests before breeding
hip_elbow_dysplasia.notes: RKC breed page (S97) good-practice tests: 'Elbow testing (for elbow dysplasia)' and 'Hip testing (for hip dysplasia)' (BVA/KC schemes); best practice: DNA test for degenerative myelopathy, eye testing. PDSA (S100): hip dysplasia leads to arthritis; elbow dysplasia screening exists (paraphrase).

degenerative_myelopathy.quote: weakness to back legs leading to paralysis
degenerative_myelopathy.notes: PDSA (S100) on DM; RKC (S97) lists a DM DNA test under best practice.

causes_of_death_2017.quote: The most common causes of death were musculoskeletal disorder (16.3%) and inability to stand (14.9%).
causes_of_death_2017.notes: O'Neill et al. 2017 (S101), same sentence on RVC news (S102). Research only — never shown in the app or register.

common_disorders_2017.value: otitis externa, osteoarthritis, diarrhoea, overweight/obesity, aggression
common_disorders_2017.quote: The most prevalent disorders were otitis externa, osteoarthritis, diarrhoea, overweight/obesity and aggression.
common_disorders_2017.notes: VetCompass news (S102, 11 Aug 2017 version). Paper (S101): overweight/obesity 5.18 %, aggression 4.76 % (males 6.75 % vs females 2.78 %) — percentages stay in research.

other_conditions.value: anal furunculosis, inherited eye disease, epilepsy, pituitary dwarfism, haemophilia A and B
other_conditions.notes: PDSA (S100) list (summarised by the tool, no verbatim quote); 'not exhaustive'.

colour_white.value: white is not a standard colour (FCI disqualifying fault)
colour_white.quote: The colour white is not allowed.
colour_white.notes: FCI disqualifying faults: 'White hair colour (also with dark eyes and nails)' and albinism. RKC breed page (S97) lists white, blue, liver and Isabella variants as non-breed-standard (NBS) colours; Colour Watch 'Category 3'. The game never draws a white, blue or liver German Shepherd.

coren_rank.notes: Coren's own top-10 list (S34, tier B, author of the book): 1 Border Collie, 2 Poodle, 3 'German Shepherd Dog', 4 Golden Retriever … (quote = the list entry as returned). Wikipedia (S35) shows the same top 10 (data.json labrador_retriever.trainability).

coren_tier.notes: Top 10 = 'Brightest' tier (ranks 1–10, S35 tier definitions).

training_notes.value: consistency; careful training and socialisation (guarding instinct)
training_notes.quote: As with all training – consistency is key!
training_notes.notes: PDSA (S100); RKC breed page (S97): used 'as a guide dog for the blind, as a tracking dog, and in obedience.'

learning_multiplier.notes: Game value — see proposed_game_parameters.german_shepherd.learning_multiplier (1.9, runbook rule).

general.value: medium-size, slightly elongated, powerful, well-muscled
general.quote: medium-size, slightly elongated, powerful and well-muscled
general.notes: FCI (S95) also 'dry bone and firm overall structure'; trunk length exceeds height 'by about 10 – 17 %'. RKC (S98): 'Slightly long in comparison to height; of powerful, well-muscled build with weather-resistant coat.' and 'balanced and free from exaggeration'.

value: black and tan / black and gold (saddle)
colours.quote: Colours are black with reddish-brown, brown and yellow to light grey markings.
colours.notes: RKC breed page (S97) breed-standard colours: 'Bi-Colour', 'Black', 'Black & Gold', 'Black & Tan', 'Dark Sable', 'Gold Sable', 'Grey', 'Grey Sable', 'Sable'. RKC standard (S98): 'Colour in itself is of secondary importance'. Never white (FCI disqualification, S95), blue, liver or Isabella (RKC NBS, S97). Frequencies: not sourced.

colour_weights.notes: UNSOURCED — game draft (verified=false in breed_appearance.php). No colour frequencies. Draw over the standard colours black-and-tan (highest weight → portrait default), sable, solid black (FCI S95, RKC S97); never white / blue / liver.

coat.value: double coat (short) or long double coat, both with undercoat
coat.quote: the hair varieties double coat and long double coat
coat.notes: RKC (S98): 'Outer coat consisting of straight, hard, close-lying hair as dense as possible; thick undercoat.' RKC breed page (S97): 'Coat length: Short & long'.

ears.value: erect, medium size, pointed
ears.quote: erect ears of medium size, which are carried upright and aligned
ears.notes: RKC (S98): 'Medium-sized, firm in texture, broad at base, set high, carried erect, almost parallel'. Tipped / drooping ears are faults (S95). One ear type → no variation.

eyes.value: dark, almond-shaped, medium size
eyes.quote: Medium-sized, almond-shaped, never protruding.
eyes.notes: RKC: 'Dark brown preferred'; FCI (S95): 'The colour of the eyes should be as dark as possible.'

tail.value: bushy, reaches the hock, hangs in a gentle sabre curve
tail.quote: Bushy-haired, reaches at least to hock.
tail.notes: RKC: 'At rest tail hangs in slight sabre-like curve'; FCI (S95): 'hanging downward in a gentle curve'.

topline_hindquarters.quote: Any tendency towards over-angulation of hindquarters, weak hocks, cow hocks or sickle hocks, highly undesirable.
topline_hindquarters.notes: RKC standard (S98): 'The topline runs without any visible break from the set on of the neck.' For PetPrep art: a level back and moderate hind legs, never the exaggerated sloping show stance (welfare rule, health.hind_conformation).

suitability._note: Source = RKC breed-page fields (S97) and PDSA (S100). Woodgreen page not reachable; AKC trait ratings not attempted (same as the earlier breeds).

rkc_grooming.quote: Grooming: More than once a week
rkc_grooming.notes: PDSA (S100): brushing or combing a few times a week (paraphrase).

pdsa_family.notes: Hedged ('some can'); PDSA adds 'dogs should always be supervised around young children' → family_pet, not children.

cavalier_king_charles_spaniel._note: Added 2026-10-10 (M5-R10-05, unattended run). Quotes as returned by the web-fetch tool on 2026-10-10; spot-check before import (sources.md S103–S110, reused S10, S11, S14, S24, S35, S45, S71). Pages were partly returned as paraphrase — only passages the tool returned in quotation marks are used as quotes. McMillan 2024 does not name the Cavalier in its text or Fig. 3 legend (S54 / LJMU full text checked 2026-10-10; Supplementary Table 3 not reachable), PMC returned a reCAPTCHA and the Dogs Trust summary (S15) does not list the breed — so the lifespan is the VetCompass breed median (S71) per the runbook rule. Woodgreen and the AKC page were not found / not attempted.

identity.value: FCI No. 136, Group 9 Section 7 (English Toy Spaniels), Great Britain
identity.quote: Group: n°9 - Chiens d'agrément et de compagnie; Section: Epagneuls anglais d'agrément; Country of origin: GRANDE-BRETAGNE
identity.notes: FCI nomenclature (S104, French-language fields as returned): standard number 136; definitive acceptance '20/01/1955'; publication of valid standard '04/11/2008'; 'Non soumise à épreuve de travail' (no working trial). FCI standard PDF (S103): 'FCI-CLASSIFICATION: Group 9 Companion and Toy Dogs' and 'Section 7 English Toy Spaniels.'; the tool returned its publication date as '08.09.2026' — differs from the nomenclature page, verify on the PDF. Quote assembled from the nomenclature fields.

weight_by_month_kg.notes: UNSOURCED — no Cavalier growth curve found.

median_uk.notes: O'Neill et al. VetCompass conference poster (SVEPM 2012, S71), Table 1 row: breed, n deaths = 121, median longevity 9.99 y, IQR 8.14–12.39. McMillan 2024 (S54) not usable for this breed (see _note) — runbook rule: else a VetCompass median. Small n, preliminary data of O'Neill 2013 (S17) → medium. Conflicts with the breed-page band 'Over 12 years' (S105, S108). Shorter than the German Shepherd (10.3), longer than the French Bulldog (9.8).

adult.quote: Exercise: Up to 1 hour per day
adult.notes: PDSA (S108): 'Your Cavalier will need at least one hour of exercise a day' (key-facts label 'Minimum exercise: 1 hour'). Sources agree on about 1 h (RKC 'up to', PDSA 'at least').

energy.value: quite energetic despite the small size
energy.quote: Despite their small size, Cavaliers are quite energetic dogs
energy.notes: RKC standard (S106): 'Sporting, affectionate, absolutely fearless.'; FCI (S103): 'Active, graceful and well balanced, with gentle expression.'

temperament.value: gay, friendly, non-aggressive, no tendency to nervousness
temperament.quote: Gay, friendly, non aggressive; no tendency to nervousness.
temperament.notes: FCI (S103): 'Sporting, affectionate, absolutely fearless. Gay, friendly, non-aggressive; no tendency towards nervousness.' PDSA (S108): 'Cavaliers are kind, gentle and loyal dogs which is why they are so popular, but will need constant company'.

family.value: known to be good around children; great family pets; supervise play
family.quote: They're known to be good around children because they're so keen to please their owners and love the company of people.
family.notes: PDSA (S108) also: 'Cavaliers are known for making really great family pets', 'Cavalier King Charles Spaniels are popular family dogs due to their small size and love of people.' and 'we would always recommend supervising your dog around children just in case playtime gets too rough'; the dog needs a place to rest away from children (S108). Explicit statement → children (supervision caveat kept here), not small_children.

time_alone.value: needs constant company; can develop separation anxiety
time_alone.quote: Like all dogs, Cavaliers prefer company and don't cope very well when left on their own.
time_alone.notes: PDSA (S108): 'Cavaliers can develop separation anxiety if their owners leave them at all' (sentence continues — paraphrase: train them to cope, never more than four hours) → no often_alone tag.

other_pets.value: tolerant, should get along with cats; prey drive with small pets
other_pets.quote: they are known for being tolerant and should get along with cats OK
other_pets.notes: PDSA (S108): 'Cavalier King Charles Spaniels can have a prey drive, so be careful of other small pets with your Cavalier' → conditional, no other_pets tag.

chewing.notes: No Cavalier-specific chewing statement found → no chews_when_bored tag.

food_motivation.notes: No Cavalier-specific food-motivation statement found. PDSA (S108) generic feeding advice: 'it's usually recommended to split their daily allowance into two meals.'; 'Treats shouldn't make up more than 10% of their recommended daily calorie intake' → no food_motivated_weight tag.

health._note: Parent-facing background only, recorded factually with sources; percentages stay here and are never shown in the app, the register export or audience docs. The breed's welfare topics in UK sources are the heart (mitral valve disease) and the skull-shape-related Chiari-like malformation / syringomyelia — RKC breed page (S105: 'can be affected by conformational concerns', heart scheme, MRI), RKC Breed Watch Category 2 (S107), PDSA (S108), University of Bristol (S110).

heart_mvd.value: heart disease (mitral valve disease) — a big problem for the breed; RKC heart scheme before breeding
heart_mvd.quote: Heart conditions (most often caused by mitral valve disease) – this is a big problem for this breed.
heart_mvd.notes: PDSA (S108): 'It is where the heart's mitral valve weakens and doesn't work as effectively, this is often first noticed as a heart murmur.' RKC breed page (S105): 'All Cavalier King Charles Spaniels that are being bred from should first be graded under The Kennel Club heart scheme.' Summers et al. 2015 (S109): heart murmur was the most common disorder — 'heart murmur (541 study dogs; 30.9% of sample group)' (percentage research only).

syringomyelia.value: Chiari-like malformation and syringomyelia (CM/SM) — painful; linked to skull shape; MRI screening
syringomyelia.quote: a very painful condition where fluid-filled areas develop within the spinal cord near the brain
syringomyelia.notes: PDSA (S108) heading 'Chiari malformation and Syringomyelia (CM/SM)'. RKC breed page (S105): 'Diagnosis for syringomyelia is by MRI scan.' University of Bristol (S110), on Mitchell et al. 2014 (Canine Genetics and Epidemiology): 'Syringomyelia (SM) is a painful condition in dogs and is more common in toy breeds.'; 'In these toy breeds, SM is usually secondary to a specific malformation of the skull'; 'The study suggests that brachycephaly, with resulting doming towards the front of the head, is associated with CM/SM.'

eyes.value: eye problems (inherited cataract, retinal dysplasia, curly coat / dry eye); protruding or irritated eyes are a Breed Watch concern
eyes.quote: Protruding eyes
eyes.notes: RKC Breed Watch Category 2 points of concern (S107): 'Signs of visible eye irritation or discomfort (including redness, discharge and tear staining)', 'Incorrect hind conformation and/or poor rear movement', 'Protruding eyes'. PDSA (S108): 'Eye problems – this includes inherited problems such as cataracts.' and 'Curly Coat/Dry Eye (CC/DE) – a condition that affects skin, coat, nails and eyes'. RKC breed page (S105): eye scheme; DNA tests for CC/DE and episodic falling. RKC standard (S106): 'Large, dark, round but not prominent'.

other_conditions.value: luxating patella, ear problems, bad teeth (shorter muzzle), episodic falling
other_conditions.quote: Bad teeth – this is a common problem in all breeds, but potentially more so in Cavaliers as they have a shorter muzzle.
other_conditions.notes: PDSA (S108) health list headings: 'Luxating patellas', 'Ear problems', 'Bad teeth', 'Episodic Falling (EF)'. PDSA: 'If you want to minimise the risk of your dog getting problems due to exaggerated features' (sentence continues — read the guide to choosing a pedigree dog, paraphrase).

common_disorders_2015.value: heart murmur, diarrhoea, dental disease, otitis externa, conjunctivitis
common_disorders_2015.notes: Summers et al. 2015 (S109), VetCompass England, 1,749 dogs with clinical entries: heart murmur 30.9 %, diarrhoea of unspecified cause 11.0 %, dental disease 9.5 %, otitis externa 9.2 %, conjunctivitis 7.5 % (as summarised by the tool). Research only — never shown in the app or register.

colour_nbs.value: chocolate & tan and chocolate tricolour are not standard colours
colour_nbs.notes: RKC breed page (S105): non-breed-standard colours 'Chocolate & Tan', 'Chocolate Tricolour'; Colour Watch 'Category 1'. FCI / RKC standards: 'Any other colour or combination of colours unacceptable.' (S103, S106). The game never draws a chocolate Cavalier.

coren_rank.notes: Wikipedia table (S35, tier C), under 'Average Working/Obedience Intelligence'. Coren's own article (S34) lists only the top and bottom 10 — the Cavalier is in neither (runbook: rank from S35). Verify in The Intelligence of Dogs.

coren_tier.quote: Understanding of new commands: 25 to 40 repetitions.; Obey first command: 50% of the time or better.;
coren_tier.notes: Tier 'Average Working/Obedience Intelligence' = ranks 40–54. Tier definitions from Wikipedia; verify in book.

training_notes.value: incredibly eager to please — fairly easy to train
training_notes.quote: Cavaliers are incredibly eager to please, which makes them fairly easy to train.
training_notes.notes: PDSA (S108).

learning_multiplier.notes: Game value — see proposed_game_parameters.cavalier_king_charles_spaniel.learning_multiplier (1.0, runbook rule).

general.value: small, active, graceful, well balanced, gentle expression
general.quote: Active, graceful and well balanced, with gentle expression.
general.notes: Same wording in FCI (S103). RKC foreword (S106): 'Breeders and judges should at all times be careful to avoid obvious conditions or exaggerations'.

colours.quote: Any other colour or combination of colours unacceptable.
colours.notes: RKC standard (S106) and FCI (S103): Black and Tan — 'raven black with tan markings above the eyes, on cheeks, inside ears, on chest and legs and underside of tail.'; Ruby — 'whole coloured rich red.'; Blenheim — 'rich chestnut markings well broken up, on pearly white ground.'; Tricolour — black and white well broken up with tan markings. RKC breed page (S105): standard colours Black & Tan, Blenheim, Ruby, Tricolour; NBS Chocolate & Tan, Chocolate Tricolour. Frequencies: not sourced.

colour_weights.notes: UNSOURCED — game draft (verified=false in breed_appearance.php). No colour frequencies. Draw over the four standard colours with Blenheim highest (portrait default), then tricolour, ruby, black and tan; never chocolate (NBS, S105).

coat.value: long, silky, free from curl, plenty of feathering
coat.quote: Long, silky, free from curl. Slight wave permissible.
coat.notes: FCI (S103): 'Long, silky, free from curl. Slight wave permissible. Plenty of feathering. Totally free from trimming.' RKC breed page (S105): 'Coat length: Medium'.

ears.value: long, set high, plenty of feather
ears.quote: Long, set high, with plenty of feather.
ears.notes: Same in FCI (S103).

eyes.value: large, dark, round but not prominent, well apart
eyes.quote: Large, dark, round but not prominent; spaced well apart.
eyes.notes: Same in FCI (S103). 'Protruding eyes' is a Breed Watch concern (S107).

nose.value: black nose, well-developed nostrils; tapered muzzle about 3.8 cm
nose.quote: Nostrils black and well developed without flesh marks.
nose.notes: FCI (S103): muzzle 'Length from base of stop to tip of nose about 1 1/2 ins. (3,8 cm). Well tapered.'; skull 'Almost flat between ears.'; stop 'Shallow.' RKC (S106): 'Skull almost flat between ears. Stop shallow.' For PetPrep art: a visible, tapered muzzle and open nostrils — never a flat face (welfare rule, health.syringomyelia).

tail.value: in balance with the body, carried happily, never much above the back
tail.quote: Length of tail in balance with body, well set on, carried happily but never much above the level of the back.
tail.notes: Same in FCI (S103). Docking (formerly optional) is not shown.

rkc_grooming.notes: PDSA (S108): 'you may find they need to be brushed daily' (sentence as returned, start).

pdsa_family.notes: PDSA also: 'Cavaliers are great little dogs that suit family environments.'

pdsa_grooming.quote: Cavalier King Charles Spaniels have fairly high maintenance coats and you may find they need to be brushed daily
